Parietal bone.r.description: One of a pair of bones forming the upper sides and roof of the cranium. Bounded by the frontal bone anteriorly, the temporal bone inferiorly, and the occipital bone posteriorly, the two parietal bones meet at the sagittal suture. Source: https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/7-2-the-skull

Parietal bone.l.description: One of a pair of bones forming the upper sides and roof of the cranium. Bounded by the frontal bone anteriorly, the temporal bone inferiorly, and the occipital bone posteriorly, the two parietal bones meet at the sagittal suture. Source: https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/7-2-the-skull

Sinus of frontal bone.description: One of a pair of air-filled cavities within the frontal bone above the eyebrows. It drains into the middle nasal meatus and, like the other paranasal sinuses, helps humidify air and lighten the skull. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/the-paranasal-sinuses

Frontal bone.description: The single bone that forms the forehead and the upper part of the eye sockets. Its midline depression between the eyebrows is the glabella, and it also forms the roof of the anterior cranial fossa. Source: https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/7-2-the-skull

Occipital bone.description: The unpaired bone forming the back and base of the skull. It contains the foramen magnum, through which the spinal cord passes, and its occipital condyles articulate with the first cervical vertebra (atlas). Source: https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/7-2-the-skull

Sinus of sphenoid bone.description: An air-filled cavity within the body of the sphenoid bone, situated close to the pituitary gland and optic nerves. It drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess of the nasal cavity. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/the-paranasal-sinuses

Sphenoid bone.description: A butterfly-shaped bone in the middle of the skull base that forms part of the walls of the eye socket and unites with nearly every other cranial bone. Its central sella turcica houses the pituitary gland. Source: https://geekymedics.com/bones-of-the-skull/

Temporal bone.r.description: A paired bone forming the lower side of the skull, made up of squamous, petrous, mastoid, and tympanic parts. The petrous portion houses the structures of the inner and middle ear, including the auditory ossicles. Source: https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/7-2-the-skull

Ethmoid bone.description: A light, spongy unpaired bone between the orbits that contributes to the nasal cavity and orbital walls. Its cribriform plate is pierced by olfactory nerve fibers, and its perpendicular plate forms part of the nasal septum. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/lateral-wall-of-the-nasal-cavity

Inferior nasal concha bone.r.description: A thin, curved paired bone forming the lowest of the three nasal conchae (turbinates) that project into the nasal cavity. It increases the surface area of the nasal mucosa to warm and humidify inhaled air. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/nasal-cavity

Lacrimal bone.r.description: The smallest and most fragile bone of the face, forming part of the medial wall of the eye socket. It contains a groove that houses the lacrimal sac, part of the tear-drainage pathway. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/nasal-cavity

Nasal bone.r.description: One of a pair of small bones that join in the midline to form the bridge of the nose. Together they connect superiorly with the frontal bone and laterally with the maxilla. Source: https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/7-2-the-skull

Maxilla.r.description: The paired bone forming the upper jaw. It carries the upper teeth, forms most of the hard palate and the floor of the eye socket, and contains the maxillary sinus, the largest paranasal sinus. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/the-paranasal-sinuses

Palatine bone.r.description: An L-shaped paired bone at the back of the nasal cavity. Its horizontal plate forms the posterior part of the hard palate, and its perpendicular plate contributes to the lateral nasal wall and orbital floor. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/nasal-cavity

Zygomatic bone.r.description: The paired cheekbone, which forms the prominence of the cheek and part of the lateral wall and floor of the eye socket. It articulates with the maxilla, temporal, sphenoid, and frontal bones. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zygomatic_bone

Mandible.description: The lower jawbone and the only movable bone of the skull. Its body carries the lower teeth, and its rami articulate with the temporal bones to form the temporomandibular joints. Source: https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/7-2-the-skull

Hyoid bone.description: A U-shaped bone in the neck that does not articulate directly with any other bone, instead being suspended by muscles and ligaments below the mandible. It anchors muscles of the tongue, floor of the mouth, and larynx. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyoid_bone

Malleus.r.description: The largest and most lateral of the three auditory ossicles in the middle ear. Its handle attaches to the eardrum and its head articulates with the incus, so vibrations of the eardrum are passed along the ossicular chain. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/malleus

Incus.r.description: The middle of the three auditory ossicles, shaped like an anvil. It connects the malleus laterally to the stapes medially, relaying sound vibrations across the middle ear. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/incus

Stapes.r.description: The smallest and lightest bone in the human body, and the most medial of the three auditory ossicles. Its footplate sits in the oval window of the inner ear, transmitting vibrations from the incus into the fluid-filled cochlea. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/stapes

Upper medial incisor.r.description: One of the eight chisel-shaped incisor teeth at the front of the mouth (four upper, four lower). Incisors have a thin cutting edge used for biting and slicing food. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/tooth-anatomy

Upper lateral incisor.r.description: One of the eight chisel-shaped incisor teeth at the front of the mouth (four upper, four lower). Incisors have a thin cutting edge used for biting and slicing food. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/tooth-anatomy

Upper canine.r.description: A single-cusped, pointed tooth located beside the lateral incisor. Canines are usually the longest teeth in the mouth and are adapted for tearing and piercing food. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/canine-tooth

Lower medial incisor.r.description: One of the eight chisel-shaped incisor teeth at the front of the mouth (four upper, four lower). Incisors have a thin cutting edge used for biting and slicing food. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/tooth-anatomy

Lower lateral incisor.r.description: One of the eight chisel-shaped incisor teeth at the front of the mouth (four upper, four lower). Incisors have a thin cutting edge used for biting and slicing food. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/tooth-anatomy

Lower canine.r.description: A single-cusped, pointed tooth located beside the lateral incisor. Canines are usually the longest teeth in the mouth and are adapted for tearing and piercing food. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/canine-tooth

Upper first premolar.r.description: A transitional tooth located between the canine and the molars, bearing at least two cusps. Premolars (bicuspids) help tear and grind food, combining features of canines and molars. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_tooth

Upper second premolar.r.description: A transitional tooth located between the canine and the molars, bearing at least two cusps. Premolars (bicuspids) help tear and grind food, combining features of canines and molars. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_tooth

Upper first molar tooth.r.description: A large, flat tooth at the back of the mouth with a broad, multi-cusped surface used mainly for grinding and crushing food during chewing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molar_(tooth)

Upper second molar tooth.r.description: A large, flat tooth at the back of the mouth with a broad, multi-cusped surface used mainly for grinding and crushing food during chewing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molar_(tooth)

Lower first premolar.r.description: A transitional tooth located between the canine and the molars, bearing at least two cusps. Premolars (bicuspids) help tear and grind food, combining features of canines and molars. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_tooth

Lower second premolar.r.description: A transitional tooth located between the canine and the molars, bearing at least two cusps. Premolars (bicuspids) help tear and grind food, combining features of canines and molars. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_tooth

Lower first molar tooth.r.description: A large, flat tooth at the back of the mouth with a broad, multi-cusped surface used mainly for grinding and crushing food during chewing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molar_(tooth)

Lower second molar tooth.r.description: A large, flat tooth at the back of the mouth with a broad, multi-cusped surface used mainly for grinding and crushing food during chewing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molar_(tooth)

Major alar cartilage.r.description: A thin, flexible plate of cartilage that curves to form the medial and lateral walls of each nostril, giving shape and support to the tip and ala (wing) of the nose. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_alar_cartilage

Lateral process of nasal septal cartilag.displayName: Right Lateral process of nasal septal cartilage
Lateral process of nasal septal cartilag.baseName: Lateral process of nasal septal cartilage
Lateral process of nasal septal cartilag.description: A flattened, triangular cartilage (also called the upper lateral cartilage) lying below the nasal bone, continuous above with the septal cartilage and connected below to the major alar cartilage. It supports the middle third of the external nose. Source: https://www.imaios.com/en/e-anatomy/anatomical-structures/nasal-septal-cartilage-1536897652

Nasal septal cartilage.description: A plate of hyaline cartilage that forms the anterior part of the nasal septum, the partition separating the two nasal cavities. It is continuous posteriorly with the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid and the vomer. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/nasal-septum

Thyroid cartilage.description: The largest cartilage of the larynx, formed by two laminae that fuse anteriorly to create the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple). It shields the vocal folds and other structures within the voice box. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/larynx

Cricoid cartilage.description: A complete, signet-ring-shaped cartilage that forms the inferior boundary of the larynx. Its narrow anterior arch and broad posterior lamina provide attachment for laryngeal muscles and ligaments. Source: https://teachmeanatomy.info/neck/viscera/larynx/laryngealcartilages/

Arytenoid cartilage.r.description: A small, paired pyramid-shaped cartilage that sits atop the cricoid cartilage at the back of the larynx. Its vocal process anchors the vocal ligament, and rotation of the cartilage opens and closes the vocal folds. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/arytenoid-cartilage

Corniculate cartilage.r.description: A small, paired conical nodule of elastic cartilage that sits atop the apex of each arytenoid cartilage, prolonging it posteriorly within the aryepiglottic fold. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corniculate_cartilage

Atlas (C1).description: The first cervical vertebra, a ring-shaped bone with no body that supports the skull. Its superior facets articulate with the occipital condyles, allowing the nodding (yes) movement of the head. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlas_(anatomy)

Vertebra C6.description: A typical cervical vertebra of the neck, characterized by a small body, a bifid spinous process, and a foramen transversarium in each transverse process that transmits the vertebral artery. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cervical_vertebrae

Vertebra C3.description: A typical cervical vertebra of the neck, characterized by a small body, a bifid spinous process, and a foramen transversarium in each transverse process that transmits the vertebral artery. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cervical_vertebrae

Vertebra C5.description: A typical cervical vertebra of the neck, characterized by a small body, a bifid spinous process, and a foramen transversarium in each transverse process that transmits the vertebral artery. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cervical_vertebrae

Vertebra C7.description: The seventh and largest cervical vertebra, known as the vertebra prominens because its long, non-bifid spinous process is easily felt at the base of the neck. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cervical_vertebrae

Vertebra C4.description: A typical cervical vertebra of the neck, characterized by a small body, a bifid spinous process, and a foramen transversarium in each transverse process that transmits the vertebral artery. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cervical_vertebrae

Vertebra T2.description: Like the other typical thoracic vertebrae, it has a heart-shaped body with costal facets for rib articulation and a long, downward-sloping spinous process. The second thoracic vertebra, larger than T1, articulates with the second rib and lies below the thoracic spinal nerve T2. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoracic_vertebrae

Vertebra T3.description: Like the other typical thoracic vertebrae, it has a heart-shaped body with costal facets for rib articulation and a long, downward-sloping spinous process. A typical mid-thoracic vertebra, articulating with the third rib and giving passage to the thoracic spinal nerve T3. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoracic_vertebrae

Vertebra T4.description: Like the other typical thoracic vertebrae, it has a heart-shaped body with costal facets for rib articulation and a long, downward-sloping spinous process. A typical mid-thoracic vertebra lying, together with T5, at the level of the sternal angle; it articulates with the fourth rib. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoracic_vertebrae

Vertebra T5.description: Like the other typical thoracic vertebrae, it has a heart-shaped body with costal facets for rib articulation and a long, downward-sloping spinous process. A typical mid-thoracic vertebra at the level of the sternal angle; the trachea typically bifurcates into the main bronchi near this level. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoracic_vertebrae

Vertebra T6.description: Like the other typical thoracic vertebrae, it has a heart-shaped body with costal facets for rib articulation and a long, downward-sloping spinous process. A typical mid-thoracic vertebra, articulating with the sixth rib and giving passage to the thoracic spinal nerve T6. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoracic_vertebrae

Vertebra T7.description: Like the other typical thoracic vertebrae, it has a heart-shaped body with costal facets for rib articulation and a long, downward-sloping spinous process. A typical mid-thoracic vertebra, articulating with the seventh rib and giving passage to the thoracic spinal nerve T7. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoracic_vertebrae

Vertebra T9.description: A thoracic vertebra that, in many people, has only a single facet (rather than the usual demi-facets) on each side for articulation with the ninth rib. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoracic_vertebrae

Vertebra T10.description: A thoracic vertebra with a single, full costal facet on each side (rather than the demi-facets typical of the vertebrae above it) for articulation with the tenth rib. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoracic_vertebrae

Vertebra T11.description: A thoracic vertebra whose body begins to resemble that of a lumbar vertebra in size and shape. It has a single costal facet, placed mainly on the pedicle, for the eleventh rib. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoracic_vertebrae

Vertebra T12.description: The last thoracic vertebra, transitional in form toward the lumbar vertebrae, with convex, laterally directed inferior articular surfaces. It bears a single costal facet for the twelfth (floating) rib. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoracic_vertebrae

Vertebra T8.description: Like the other typical thoracic vertebrae, it has a heart-shaped body with costal facets for rib articulation and a long, downward-sloping spinous process. A typical thoracic vertebra lying, together with T9, near the level of the xiphisternal joint. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoracic_vertebrae

Vertebra T1.description: The first thoracic vertebra, transitional in shape between a cervical and thoracic vertebra. It bears a full costal facet for the head of the first rib and a demi-facet for the second rib. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebra

Vertebra L1.description: One of the five lumbar vertebrae between the rib cage and pelvis. Lumbar vertebrae are the largest of the movable vertebrae, with a large kidney-shaped body and no foramen transversarium or facets for ribs, reflecting their weight-bearing role. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lumbar_vertebrae

Coccyx.description: The tailbone, a small triangular bone at the very bottom of the spine formed by the fusion of three to five rudimentary vertebrae. Though largely vestigial, it serves as an attachment site for several pelvic floor muscles and ligaments. Source: https://louis.pressbooks.pub/anatomylab/chapter/lab-5-vertebral-column-bony-thorax-and-forelimb-bones/

Fifth rib.r.description: A typical true rib: a long, curved bone that articulates posteriorly with the vertebral column and anteriorly, via its own costal cartilage, directly with the sternum. Source: https://teachmeanatomy.info/thorax/bones/ribcage/

First rib.r.description: The shortest and most sharply curved of the ribs, and the widest relative to its length. Unlike the ribs below it, it lies almost horizontally and has only one facet for articulation with the vertebral body of T1. Source: https://teachmeanatomy.info/thorax/bones/ribcage/

Fourth rib.r.description: A typical true rib: a long, curved bone that articulates posteriorly with the vertebral column and anteriorly, via its own costal cartilage, directly with the sternum. Source: https://teachmeanatomy.info/thorax/bones/ribcage/

Second rib.r.description: A true rib, longer than the first but with a similar sharp curvature. It is thinner and less horizontal than the first rib and provides attachment for part of the serratus anterior muscle. Source: https://teachmeanatomy.info/thorax/bones/ribcage/

Seventh rib.r.description: A typical true rib: a long, curved bone that articulates posteriorly with the vertebral column and anteriorly, via its own costal cartilage, directly with the sternum. Source: https://teachmeanatomy.info/thorax/bones/ribcage/

Sixth rib.r.description: A typical true rib: a long, curved bone that articulates posteriorly with the vertebral column and anteriorly, via its own costal cartilage, directly with the sternum. Source: https://teachmeanatomy.info/thorax/bones/ribcage/

Third rib.r.description: A typical true rib: a long, curved bone that articulates posteriorly with the vertebral column and anteriorly, via its own costal cartilage, directly with the sternum. Source: https://teachmeanatomy.info/thorax/bones/ribcage/

Eleventh rib.r.description: A floating rib: it articulates posteriorly with the vertebral column but has no anterior attachment to the sternum or to another rib, ending instead in the musculature of the abdominal wall. Source: https://www.imaios.com/en/e-anatomy/anatomical-structures/costal-cartilages-1537019452

Twelfth rib.r.description: A floating rib: it articulates posteriorly with the vertebral column but has no anterior attachment to the sternum or to another rib, ending instead in the musculature of the abdominal wall. Source: https://www.imaios.com/en/e-anatomy/anatomical-structures/costal-cartilages-1537019452

Eighth rib.r.description: A false rib: it articulates posteriorly with the vertebral column, but anteriorly its costal cartilage attaches to the cartilage of the rib above rather than directly to the sternum. Source: https://www.imaios.com/en/e-anatomy/anatomical-structures/costal-cartilages-1537019452

Ninth rib.r.description: A false rib: it articulates posteriorly with the vertebral column, but anteriorly its costal cartilage attaches to the cartilage of the rib above rather than directly to the sternum. Source: https://www.imaios.com/en/e-anatomy/anatomical-structures/costal-cartilages-1537019452

Tenth rib.r.description: A false rib: it articulates posteriorly with the vertebral column, but anteriorly its costal cartilage attaches to the cartilage of the rib above rather than directly to the sternum. Source: https://www.imaios.com/en/e-anatomy/anatomical-structures/costal-cartilages-1537019452

Manubrium of sternum.description: The broad, trapezoid-shaped upper part of the sternum. Its superior border forms the jugular notch, and it articulates with the clavicles, the first ribs, and part of the second costal cartilage. Source: https://teachmeanatomy.info/thorax/bones/sternum/

Xiphoid process.description: The small, variably shaped cartilaginous-to-bony tip at the lower end of the sternum. It does not fully ossify until adulthood and serves as a landmark for correct hand placement during chest compressions. Source: https://teachmeanatomy.info/thorax/bones/sternum/

Body of sternum.description: The long, flat middle portion of the sternum, also called the gladiolus. It articulates with the manubrium above and the xiphoid process below, and its lateral borders carry facets for the costal cartilages of ribs three through seven. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/sternum

Clavicle.r.description: The collarbone: a slender, S-shaped long bone that struts the shoulder blade away from the sternum. It is the only long bone that lies horizontally and is also the most commonly fractured bone in the body. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavicle

Humerus.r.description: The long bone of the upper arm, running from the shoulder to the elbow. Its rounded head articulates with the scapula to form the shoulder joint, and its lower end articulates with the radius and ulna at the elbow. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humerus

Patella.r.description: The kneecap, the largest sesamoid bone in the body. It sits within the quadriceps tendon in front of the knee joint and increases the mechanical leverage of the thigh muscles during knee extension. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patella

Talus.r.description: The bone that connects the leg to the foot, articulating with the tibia and fibula above to form the ankle joint and with the calcaneus below. It transmits the body's weight from the leg to the foot. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/tarsal-bones

Calcaneus.r.description: The heel bone, the largest of the tarsal bones. It articulates with the talus above and the cuboid in front, and provides attachment for the Achilles tendon at its posterior tuberosity. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/tarsal-bones

Navicular bone.r.description: A boat-shaped tarsal bone of the midfoot, positioned between the talus behind and the three cuneiform bones in front. It contributes to the medial longitudinal arch of the foot. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/tarsal-bones

Cuboid bone.r.description: The most lateral tarsal bone of the distal row, located between the calcaneus and the fourth and fifth metatarsals. Its plantar surface carries a groove for the tendon of fibularis (peroneus) longus. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/cuboid

Medial cuneiform bone.r.description: The largest and most medial of the three cuneiform bones, located between the navicular and the first metatarsal bone. Source: https://www.getbodysmart.com/lower-limb-bones/tarsals/

First metacarpal bone.r.description: One of five long bones in the palm that connect the carpal bones of the wrist to the phalanges of the fingers, numbered one (thumb) through five (little finger) from lateral to medial. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacarpal_bones

Second metacarpal bone.r.description: One of five long bones in the palm that connect the carpal bones of the wrist to the phalanges of the fingers, numbered one (thumb) through five (little finger) from lateral to medial. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacarpal_bones

Fifth metacarpal bone.r.description: One of five long bones in the palm that connect the carpal bones of the wrist to the phalanges of the fingers, numbered one (thumb) through five (little finger) from lateral to medial. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacarpal_bones

Capitate bone.r.description: The largest carpal bone, positioned in the center of the distal row. It articulates with the third metacarpal as well as several neighboring carpal bones, anchoring the central column of the wrist. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitate_bone

Hamate bone.r.description: A wedge-shaped carpal bone on the little-finger side of the distal row, named for the hook-like process (hamulus) that projects from its palmar surface and provides attachment for the transverse carpal ligament. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK535382/

Lunate bone.r.description: A crescent-shaped carpal bone in the middle of the proximal row, between the scaphoid and triquetrum. It articulates with the radius above and helps form the wrist joint. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunate_bone

Pisiform bone.r.description: A small, pea-shaped carpal bone on the palmar surface of the triquetrum. It is a sesamoid bone embedded in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris and does not directly participate in the wrist joint. Source: https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1899456-overview

Scaphoid bone.r.description: The largest carpal bone of the proximal row, boat-shaped and located at the base of the thumb side of the wrist. It bridges the two carpal rows and is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/carpal-bones

Trapezium bone.r.description: A carpal bone of the distal row, located at the base of the thumb. Its saddle-shaped surface articulates with the first metacarpal, forming the highly mobile joint at the base of the thumb. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK535382/

Trapezoid bone.r.description: The smallest carpal bone of the distal row, wedged between the trapezium and the capitate. It articulates distally with the base of the second metacarpal. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK535382/

Triquetrum bone.r.description: A pyramid-shaped carpal bone on the little-finger side of the proximal row. It articulates with the lunate, the pisiform, and the hamate bone. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/carpal-bones

Axis (C2).description: The second cervical vertebra, distinguished by a bony peg called the dens (odontoid process) that projects upward into the ring of the atlas, forming a pivot that allows side-to-side rotation of the head. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_(anatomy)

Scapula.r.description: The shoulder blade: a flat, triangular bone on the back of the rib cage that provides attachment for many muscles of the shoulder and forms the glenoid cavity, which articulates with the head of the humerus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scapula

Radius.r.description: The lateral bone of the forearm (on the thumb side), which rotates around the ulna to allow the palm to turn up or down. Its head articulates with the humerus and its distal end forms most of the wrist joint. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radius_(bone)

Ulna.r.description: The medial, longer bone of the forearm, on the little-finger side. Its proximal olecranon process forms the point of the elbow, and it articulates with the humerus and radius. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulna

Femur.r.description: The thigh bone, the longest and strongest bone in the body. Its rounded head articulates with the acetabulum of the hip bone, and its distal end articulates with the tibia and patella to form the knee joint. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femur

Hip bone.r.description: The large, irregular bone of the pelvis formed by the fusion of the ilium, ischium, and pubis. Its cup-shaped acetabulum articulates with the femur, and it joins its counterpart anteriorly and the sacrum posteriorly. Source: https://teachmeanatomy.info/pelvis/bones/

Tibia.r.description: The shinbone, the larger and stronger of the two bones of the lower leg, bearing most of the body's weight. Its upper end articulates with the femur at the knee and its lower end with the talus at the ankle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibia

Fibula.r.description: The slender, laterally positioned bone of the lower leg. It bears little body weight but provides muscle attachment and forms the lateral malleolus, stabilizing the outer side of the ankle joint. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibula

Sacrum.description: A large, triangular bone formed by the fusion of five sacral vertebrae, located at the base of the spine between the two hip bones. It transmits the weight of the upper body to the pelvis and forms the posterior wall of the pelvic cavity. Source: https://teachmeanatomy.info/pelvis/bones/

Temporal bone.l.description: A paired bone forming the lower side of the skull, made up of squamous, petrous, mastoid, and tympanic parts. The petrous portion houses the structures of the inner and middle ear, including the auditory ossicles. Source: https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/7-2-the-skull

Inferior nasal concha bone.l.description: A thin, curved paired bone forming the lowest of the three nasal conchae (turbinates) that project into the nasal cavity. It increases the surface area of the nasal mucosa to warm and humidify inhaled air. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/nasal-cavity

Lacrimal bone.l.description: The smallest and most fragile bone of the face, forming part of the medial wall of the eye socket. It contains a groove that houses the lacrimal sac, part of the tear-drainage pathway. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/nasal-cavity

Nasal bone.l.description: One of a pair of small bones that join in the midline to form the bridge of the nose. Together they connect superiorly with the frontal bone and laterally with the maxilla. Source: https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology-2e/pages/7-2-the-skull

Vomer.description: A thin, unpaired bone forming the lower and back part of the nasal septum. It sits in the midline and articulates with the sphenoid, ethmoid, palatine, and maxillary bones. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vomer

Maxilla.l.description: The paired bone forming the upper jaw. It carries the upper teeth, forms most of the hard palate and the floor of the eye socket, and contains the maxillary sinus, the largest paranasal sinus. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/the-paranasal-sinuses

Palatine bone.l.description: An L-shaped paired bone at the back of the nasal cavity. Its horizontal plate forms the posterior part of the hard palate, and its perpendicular plate contributes to the lateral nasal wall and orbital floor. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/nasal-cavity

Zygomatic bone.l.description: The paired cheekbone, which forms the prominence of the cheek and part of the lateral wall and floor of the eye socket. It articulates with the maxilla, temporal, sphenoid, and frontal bones. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zygomatic_bone

Malleus.l.description: The largest and most lateral of the three auditory ossicles in the middle ear. Its handle attaches to the eardrum and its head articulates with the incus, so vibrations of the eardrum are passed along the ossicular chain. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/malleus

Incus.l.description: The middle of the three auditory ossicles, shaped like an anvil. It connects the malleus laterally to the stapes medially, relaying sound vibrations across the middle ear. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/incus

Stapes.l.description: The smallest and lightest bone in the human body, and the most medial of the three auditory ossicles. Its footplate sits in the oval window of the inner ear, transmitting vibrations from the incus into the fluid-filled cochlea. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/stapes

Upper medial incisor.l.description: One of the eight chisel-shaped incisor teeth at the front of the mouth (four upper, four lower). Incisors have a thin cutting edge used for biting and slicing food. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/tooth-anatomy

Upper lateral incisor.l.description: One of the eight chisel-shaped incisor teeth at the front of the mouth (four upper, four lower). Incisors have a thin cutting edge used for biting and slicing food. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/tooth-anatomy

Upper canine.l.description: A single-cusped, pointed tooth located beside the lateral incisor. Canines are usually the longest teeth in the mouth and are adapted for tearing and piercing food. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/canine-tooth

Lower medial incisor.l.description: One of the eight chisel-shaped incisor teeth at the front of the mouth (four upper, four lower). Incisors have a thin cutting edge used for biting and slicing food. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/tooth-anatomy

Lower lateral incisor.l.description: One of the eight chisel-shaped incisor teeth at the front of the mouth (four upper, four lower). Incisors have a thin cutting edge used for biting and slicing food. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/tooth-anatomy

Lower canine.l.description: A single-cusped, pointed tooth located beside the lateral incisor. Canines are usually the longest teeth in the mouth and are adapted for tearing and piercing food. Source: https://www.britannica.com/science/canine-tooth

Upper first premolar.l.description: A transitional tooth located between the canine and the molars, bearing at least two cusps. Premolars (bicuspids) help tear and grind food, combining features of canines and molars. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_tooth

Upper second premolar.l.description: A transitional tooth located between the canine and the molars, bearing at least two cusps. Premolars (bicuspids) help tear and grind food, combining features of canines and molars. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_tooth

Upper first molar tooth.l.description: A large, flat tooth at the back of the mouth with a broad, multi-cusped surface used mainly for grinding and crushing food during chewing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molar_(tooth)

Upper second molar tooth.l.description: A large, flat tooth at the back of the mouth with a broad, multi-cusped surface used mainly for grinding and crushing food during chewing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molar_(tooth)

Lower second molar tooth.l.description: A large, flat tooth at the back of the mouth with a broad, multi-cusped surface used mainly for grinding and crushing food during chewing. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molar_(tooth)

Major alar cartilage.l.description: A thin, flexible plate of cartilage that curves to form the medial and lateral walls of each nostril, giving shape and support to the tip and ala (wing) of the nose. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_alar_cartilage

Lateral process of nasal septal cartilag.description: A flattened, triangular cartilage (also called the upper lateral cartilage) lying below the nasal bone, continuous above with the septal cartilage and connected below to the major alar cartilage. It supports the middle third of the external nose. Source: https://www.imaios.com/en/e-anatomy/anatomical-structures/nasal-septal-cartilage-1536897652

Arytenoid cartilage.l.description: A small, paired pyramid-shaped cartilage that sits atop the cricoid cartilage at the back of the larynx. Its vocal process anchors the vocal ligament, and rotation of the cartilage opens and closes the vocal folds. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/arytenoid-cartilage

Corniculate cartilage.l.description: A small, paired conical nodule of elastic cartilage that sits atop the apex of each arytenoid cartilage, prolonging it posteriorly within the aryepiglottic fold. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corniculate_cartilage

Clavicle.l.description: The collarbone: a slender, S-shaped long bone that struts the shoulder blade away from the sternum. It is the only long bone that lies horizontally and is also the most commonly fractured bone in the body. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavicle

Humerus.l.description: The long bone of the upper arm, running from the shoulder to the elbow. Its rounded head articulates with the scapula to form the shoulder joint, and its lower end articulates with the radius and ulna at the elbow. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humerus

Patella.l.description: The kneecap, the largest sesamoid bone in the body. It sits within the quadriceps tendon in front of the knee joint and increases the mechanical leverage of the thigh muscles during knee extension. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patella

Talus.l.description: The bone that connects the leg to the foot, articulating with the tibia and fibula above to form the ankle joint and with the calcaneus below. It transmits the body's weight from the leg to the foot. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/tarsal-bones

Calcaneus.l.description: The heel bone, the largest of the tarsal bones. It articulates with the talus above and the cuboid in front, and provides attachment for the Achilles tendon at its posterior tuberosity. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/tarsal-bones

Navicular bone.l.description: A boat-shaped tarsal bone of the midfoot, positioned between the talus behind and the three cuneiform bones in front. It contributes to the medial longitudinal arch of the foot. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/tarsal-bones

Cuboid bone.l.description: The most lateral tarsal bone of the distal row, located between the calcaneus and the fourth and fifth metatarsals. Its plantar surface carries a groove for the tendon of fibularis (peroneus) longus. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/cuboid

Capitate bone.l.description: The largest carpal bone, positioned in the center of the distal row. It articulates with the third metacarpal as well as several neighboring carpal bones, anchoring the central column of the wrist. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitate_bone

Hamate bone.l.description: A wedge-shaped carpal bone on the little-finger side of the distal row, named for the hook-like process (hamulus) that projects from its palmar surface and provides attachment for the transverse carpal ligament. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK535382/

Lunate bone.l.description: A crescent-shaped carpal bone in the middle of the proximal row, between the scaphoid and triquetrum. It articulates with the radius above and helps form the wrist joint. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunate_bone

Pisiform bone.l.description: A small, pea-shaped carpal bone on the palmar surface of the triquetrum. It is a sesamoid bone embedded in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris and does not directly participate in the wrist joint. Source: https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/1899456-overview

Scaphoid bone.l.description: The largest carpal bone of the proximal row, boat-shaped and located at the base of the thumb side of the wrist. It bridges the two carpal rows and is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/carpal-bones

Trapezium bone.l.description: A carpal bone of the distal row, located at the base of the thumb. Its saddle-shaped surface articulates with the first metacarpal, forming the highly mobile joint at the base of the thumb. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK535382/

Trapezoid bone.l.description: The smallest carpal bone of the distal row, wedged between the trapezium and the capitate. It articulates distally with the base of the second metacarpal. Source: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK535382/

Triquetrum bone.l.description: A pyramid-shaped carpal bone on the little-finger side of the proximal row. It articulates with the lunate, the pisiform, and the hamate bone. Source: https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/anatomy/carpal-bones

Scapula.l.description: The shoulder blade: a flat, triangular bone on the back of the rib cage that provides attachment for many muscles of the shoulder and forms the glenoid cavity, which articulates with the head of the humerus. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scapula

Radius.l.description: The lateral bone of the forearm (on the thumb side), which rotates around the ulna to allow the palm to turn up or down. Its head articulates with the humerus and its distal end forms most of the wrist joint. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radius_(bone)

Ulna.l.description: The medial, longer bone of the forearm, on the little-finger side. Its proximal olecranon process forms the point of the elbow, and it articulates with the humerus and radius. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulna

Femur.l.description: The thigh bone, the longest and strongest bone in the body. Its rounded head articulates with the acetabulum of the hip bone, and its distal end articulates with the tibia and patella to form the knee joint. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femur

Hip bone.l.description: The large, irregular bone of the pelvis formed by the fusion of the ilium, ischium, and pubis. Its cup-shaped acetabulum articulates with the femur, and it joins its counterpart anteriorly and the sacrum posteriorly. Source: https://teachmeanatomy.info/pelvis/bones/

Tibia.l.description: The shinbone, the larger and stronger of the two bones of the lower leg, bearing most of the body's weight. Its upper end articulates with the femur at the knee and its lower end with the talus at the ankle. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibia

Fibula.l.description: The slender, laterally positioned bone of the lower leg. It bears little body weight but provides muscle attachment and forms the lateral malleolus, stabilizing the outer side of the ankle joint. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibula

Posterior cells of ethmoid bone.l.displayName: Left Posterior cells of ethmoid bone
Posterior cells of ethmoid bone.l.description: A group of roughly six air-filled cavities within the posterior part of the ethmoid bone's labyrinth. They drain into the superior nasal meatus, close to the sphenoid sinus. Source: https://www.imaios.com/en/e-anatomy/anatomical-structures/posterior-ethmoidal-cells-1541214124

Middle cells of ethmoid bone.l.displayName: Left Middle cells of ethmoid bone
Middle cells of ethmoid bone.l.description: A group of air-filled cavities within the middle part of the ethmoid bone's labyrinth. They open onto the surface of the ethmoidal bulla within the middle nasal meatus. Source: https://www.imaios.com/en/e-anatomy/anatomical-structures/cells-of-ethmoid-bone-1536896848

Anterior cells of ethmoid bone.l.displayName: Left Anterior cells of ethmoid bone
Anterior cells of ethmoid bone.l.description: A cluster of roughly 11 small air-filled cavities within the anterior part of the ethmoid bone's labyrinth. They drain into the middle nasal meatus via the ethmoidal infundibulum. Source: https://www.imaios.com/en/e-anatomy/anatomical-structures/anterior-cells-of-ethmoid-bone-1536896856

They drain into the superior nasal meatus, close to the sphenoid sinus. Source: https://www.imaios.com/en/e-anatomy/anatomical-structures/posterior-ethmoidal-cells-1541214124

Anterior cells of ethmoid bone.r.description: A cluster of roughly 11 small air-filled cavities within the anterior part of the ethmoid bone's labyrinth. Eighth rib.l.description: A false rib: it articulates posteriorly with the vertebral column, but anteriorly its costal cartilage attaches to the cartilage of the rib above rather than directly to the sternum. Source: https://www.imaios.com/en/e-anatomy/anatomical-structures/costal-cartilages-1537019452
